leading_positions.synthesis: Four members prefer a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, and all four name the same two laureates, Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. They share the view that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea, that accuracy near 10^-18 is reproduced and cross-compared between institutions, and that the citation should be drawn tightly around the lattice clock and leave out the Th-229 nuclear clock. They differ in emphasis and in how firmly they hold it: Johansson moved here from circuit QED and says his ranking rests on colleagues' judgement in atomic physics, and the Chair also moved here from IceCube. Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth each describe some version of the concern that this is metrology next to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, but they weigh it differently. Not shared: how much credit Takamoto, Lemonde and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups deserve. The four statements do not settle this, and several members say they have not checked the priority record.

Two members prefer a single-part prize for topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect, naming Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Eriksson ranks it first from the outset. Mehlig moved to it from KPZ (B017), which no colleague supported in round 1. Both frame the citation around the Z2 invariant and the HgTe realisation to keep it separate from the 2016 topological-phases prize, and both accept that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D work of Fu, Hasan and others, are outside the trio. Not shared: how serious the credit gap is. Mehlig says the committee must be ready to explain the omission of Bernevig and Hughes, while Eriksson would rather not stretch the prize to add names. Kroll and Pearce name B036 as an alternative, but they do not prefer it.

Danielsson alone prefers the experimental Higgs discovery with ATLAS and CMS (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee). He holds it with less confidence than in his opening ballot and names B036 and B025 as fallbacks if the expert reports cannot support these three names. Lindroth and Mehlig both state difficulty with crediting a few individuals in collaborations of thousands. He also raises the question of whether this would be the experimental half of the 2013 prize.

Olsson alone prefers spherical-aberration correction in electron microscopy (Rose, Urban, Haider). She says openly that she is a biased judge as a microscopist. She makes her position conditional on settling whether the TEM corrector work and the Krivanek, Dellby and Batson STEM corrector work are one invention or two, and says she would not block B025 and would move to it if the priority of the first Sr lattice-clock demonstration is confirmed.

areas_of_agreement: All eight round-1 files prefer a single-part prize, so no member has proposed a two-part configuration. Mehlig and Eriksson raise the idea of a combined prize, but the three-laureate cap makes it hard.

For B025, the four members who prefer it name the same two laureates. Olsson, Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig do not contest the two names, and Danielsson, Eriksson, Olsson and Mehlig each list B025 as an alternative or as acceptable. Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson also say they could support or accept it.

Members who prefer other ballots generally call B025 mature and cleanly attributed (Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig, Olsson) and call B036 mature with a stable interpretation (Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth, Pearce), though each attaches a stated reservation.
Several members say that the citation, not just the laureate list, must be drawn tightly: lattice clock only for B025, and Z2 invariant plus HgTe realisation for B036.

IceCube (B007) and circuit QED (B016) are no longer preferred by anyone in round 1. Pearce and Johansson, who opened with them first, both moved. Several members give timing reasons: unidentified sources for B007, and proximity to the 2025 prize for B016.
scientific_disputes: Whether an optical lattice clock at 10^-18 is a physics discovery or an enabling precision-metrology tool. Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and Pearce point to relativistic geodesy, constants tests and dark-matter searches. Mehlig, Danielsson and Olsson ask whether the physics delivered so far is capability and bounds rather than a new fact about nature.

Whether the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant are a distinct achievement from the 2016 prize on topological phases or a later chapter of the same story. Eriksson and Mehlig say the time-reversal-invariant Z2 class was not covered by 2016, and Danielsson partly agrees. Lindroth ranked B036 lower because of the overlap, and Pearce names the 2016 prize as background to the omission problem.
Whether the physics of B025 is separable from the 2005 comb prize, given that Ye's clocks depend on the comb. Mehlig, Eriksson, Lindroth and Olsson raise this directly.
Whether discovery by nature (B003) outweighs other criteria, and whether a collaboration discovery would be read as the experimental half of the 2013 prize.
attribution_disputes: B025: Takamoto and Lemonde (and SYRTE, PTB and NIST) are named by Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce as possible additional claims. Kroll treats Takamoto's Sr demonstration as part of Katori's own group's credit. Lindroth and Olsson say the original demonstration, not the most precise one, should be the test. No one has checked the priority record.

B036: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe effect that Molenkamp measured. Zhang died in 2018, but Hughes and Bernevig are alive and the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Roy and Hasan is also left out. Eriksson, Mehlig, Danielsson and Pearce all note these gaps. Pearce asks whether the trio can be defended as it stands.
B003: Danielsson, Lindroth and Mehlig all see the use of the founding spokespersons of ATLAS and CMS as a proxy and not as a demonstrated identification of who was decisive.
B008: Krivanek, Dellby and Batson (STEM corrector) are a competing claim to Rose, Haider and Urban (TEM corrector).

B007, B016, B022 and B017 are not preferred by anyone but are mentioned in discussion. For B016 the third name (Blais or Girvin) is unresolved, and for B022 the experimental credit (Cao and others) is unresolved. For B017, Mehlig notes that Parisi's 2021 prize complicates the credit.
maturity_disputes: B025 is described by its supporters as mature and independently reproduced, but nobody says maturity is the problem. The open question is whether it is a discovery.
B036 is described by Eriksson and Mehlig as confirmed for more than fifteen years, but Lindroth and others question whether it is timely or an extension of 2016.

B007 is not preferred by anyone in round 1: Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig and Pearce see the diffuse flux as established but source identification as still evolving, so the question is whether a prize would be a few years early.

B022 is described by Lindroth, Eriksson and Olsson as strong and young, with the pairing mechanism unsettled. Olsson says the discovery of the phases is firm, while Mehlig and Eriksson say recognition may be early.
B016: Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth all raise timing after the 2025 prize, and Johansson says he cannot judge the distance objectively.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson: directs the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and works with superconducting-circuit groups, so he says he should not drive any decision on B016 and, to a lesser degree, B009. He discloses no connection to Katori, Ye or B037.

Kroll: spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during his PhD, and Hall was Ye's mentor at JILA. He describes this as a mentor-lineage link and not a collaboration, and leaves the question of recusal on B025 to the Chair. He also notes his WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Johansson.
Olsson: an electron microscopist and President of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, so she works in the field of B008 and accepts a recusal discussion on it.
Lindroth: a long-time collaborator of L'Huillier and close to the field of atomic structure theory, with the atom-optics community around B037 overlapping hers. She reports no link to Katori or Ye.

Pearce (Chair): no tie to B025. For B007 he works in the same broad astroparticle field and the Fermi-LAT collaboration took part in TXS 0506+056 follow-up, with no personal tie to IceCube, Halzen or Spiering.
Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig report no specific conflict. Eriksson and Mehlig note that any later link to B036 candidates, or to Gothenburg colleagues, would be flagged.
questions_for_round2: B025: who first demonstrated the Sr lattice clock at a level that proved the idea, what do Takamoto, Lemonde, and Ludlow's contributions add, and does that change the two names Katori and Ye or leave the citation unchanged?

B025: what is the exact citation wording that separates the magic-wavelength lattice clock from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and keeps the Th-229 nuclear clock out? Can Lindroth confirm that the lattice light-shift and blackbody evaluation is robust enough to support the 10^-18 claim?
B025: Kroll's conflict note on Hall and Ye. Does the committee judge this to require recusal or only disclosure?

B036: can the committee defend Kane, Mele and Molenkamp without Bernevig, Hughes (and the late Zhang), and what exact citation keeps the Z2 invariant and HgTe realisation distinct from the 2016 prize?

Discovery versus capability: does the committee want to rank B025 on the same footing as B036 and B003, or is a measurement-capability prize a lower priority in a year with such candidates? What would Mehlig, Danielsson and Olsson need to see to move?
B003: can the expert reports support the founding spokespersons as the right three names? If not, does Danielsson move to B025 or B036?
B008: are the TEM and STEM corrector claims one invention or two, and does Olsson hold B008 as her preference or move toward B025?
Are the four preferred ballots mutually exclusive in practice, or does anyone propose a configuration with more than one prize part given the three-laureate cap?
summary.chair_observation: In round 1, four members prefer B025, two prefer B036, and one each prefers B003 and B008. The B025 group names identical laureates, but the case against it (metrology, overlap with 2005 and 2012, early-contributor credit) is stated by its own supporters as well as by Mehlig and Olsson, and it is not yet answered in the ballots. The B036 group is smaller, but its main weakness, the omitted Bernevig and Hughes, is also stated by its own supporters. As Chair I moved from B007 to B025 after reading the openings and I note that I defer to the atomic and condensed-matter members on both leading cases. This summary does not rule on either, and the points above remain for round 2.
